title: How Disease Damages Farm Production: Myrtle Rust and Foot-and-Mouth
subtitle: How does disease damage farm production, and why does the bill so often reach far past the sick plants and animals?
subject: Biology
lessonIntent: stating the three things disease needs (pathogen, a host it can infect, the right conditions); explaining how a paddock of one variety and the movement of plants and soil raise the risk; describing direct effects on crops (yield, quality, control costs) with mechanisms for rust and nematodes; assessing myrtle rust (cause: an introduced rust fungus meeting myrtles with little resistance, spread by wind and nursery plants; effects on lemon myrtle and tea tree plantations, on native species, and permanence); describing foot-and-mouth disease (virus, cloven-hoofed animals, spread, blisters, reduced milk and meat, low adult death rate); separating direct effects (in the sick animals) from indirect effects (control and closed markets) with the 2001 United Kingdom outbreak; explaining why indirect effects usually dominate for an exporter like Australia; assessing an effect by size, duration and reach; distinguishing direct and indirect effects in an unseen outbreak and giving biological and agricultural causes of crop losses.

voiceover.text: In April 2010, a rust fungus turned up on plants at one nursery on the New South Wales Central Coast. Within a few years it had spread the length of the east coast, on eucalypts, paperbarks and lemon myrtle. So how does disease damage farm production, and why does the bill so often reach far past the sick plants and animals?

Start with causes. For a disease to strike, three things have to meet: a pathogen, a host it can infect, and the right conditions. Rust spores, for example, need a film of water on the leaf to germinate, so wet weather and heavy dew raise the risk. Crops face the same pathogen groups you met earlier: fungi, bacteria, viruses and nematodes.

Farming can tip the odds. Remember the Cavendish banana: every plant is a clone, so they all share one weakness. A paddock of a single variety is similar. A pathogen that can infect one plant can infect the next, with no resistant plants in between to slow it. Moving plants, soil and machinery carries pathogens to new districts too. So the causes are partly biology and partly farming, and the farming part can be changed.

What does disease cost a crop? First, yield. Rust pustules take sugars from the leaf and destroy green tissue, so the plant makes less food and fills less grain. Root-knot nematodes swell the roots into galls that squeeze the xylem, the tubes that carry water up, so the plant wilts even in moist soil. Second, quality: shrivelled grain or marked fruit sells at a lower grade. Third, cost: fungicides, resistant varieties and replanting.

Now a real case. Myrtle rust is caused by a fungus native to South and Central America. It attacks the myrtle family, which includes eucalypts, paperbarks, tea tree and lemon myrtle. Australian myrtles had never met this fungus, so many species had little resistance. Its spores travel on the wind, and infected nursery plants carried it long distances, fast.

It has since been found in Tasmania, the Northern Territory and, in 2022, northern Western Australia. Lemon myrtle and tea tree are grown in dense rows of one species, which suits the fungus, so growers now pay for fungicide, and untreated plantations can lose much of their crop. The damage runs past the farm too. The native guava, once a common rainforest shrub, is now critically endangered. And this rust can't be eradicated, so the costs don't end after one season.

Animals next. Foot-and-mouth disease is caused by a virus that infects cloven-hoofed animals: cattle, sheep, pigs and goats. It spreads by contact, through the air, and on vehicles, boots and feed. The virus causes blisters in the mouth and on the feet, so animals stop eating, go lame, and make less milk and meat. Most adults survive. These are the direct effects: losses in the sick animals themselves.

Follow the bill. In 2001, foot-and-mouth disease spread through Britain. To stop it, over six million animals were killed, most of them never infected: whole herds on infected and neighbouring farms were culled, and animals stranded by movement bans, short of feed and space, were killed for welfare. Export markets closed, and the countryside was shut to visitors. The total came to about eight billion pounds, and tourism lost about as much as farming and the food industry. These are indirect effects: costs beyond the sick animals, from control and closed markets.

Australia has been free of foot-and-mouth disease since 1872, and it sells most of its beef overseas, about three-quarters. One confirmed case would stop exports to many markets straight away. In 2022, government economists estimated a large outbreak could cost about 80 billion dollars over ten years, mostly through lost exports. That's why, for an exporter, the indirect effects usually outweigh the direct ones.

So how do you assess an effect? Ask how big it is, how long it lasts, and how far it reaches. Rust in one wheat season costs that harvest. A pathogen that settles in for good, like myrtle rust, changes what can be grown for years. And a disease that closes markets reaches far beyond the farms that had it.
So when you assess a disease, count past the farm gate. The sick plant or animal is only the first cost. Control, markets and ecosystems are the rest.

Two exam questions. First. A country that exports most of its beef has been free of foot-and-mouth disease for decades. The disease is confirmed in one herd of 40 cattle. All 40 are culled, along with 2,000 healthy cattle on nearby farms, and three trading partners suspend imports of its beef. Distinguish between the direct and indirect effects of this outbreak, and explain which is likely to cost more. Pause here to answer.

Direct effects are losses in the infected herd: the 40 sick cattle, producing less, then culled. Indirect effects come from control and trade: the 2,000 healthy cattle culled, and the lost beef exports. The indirect effects will likely cost far more, because the country exports most of its beef. Counting the healthy cattle as a direct effect is the classic mistake.

Second. Nearly every farm in a district grows the same wheat variety. A new strain of a rust fungus appears that can infect this variety. Its spores travel on the wind, and the season is warm and wet. Yields fall across the whole district. Explain one biological cause and one agricultural cause of these losses. Pause here to answer.

Biological: the new strain can infect this variety, and wind spreads its spores. Wet weather helps them germinate. Agricultural: every farm grows the same variety, so every paddock is equally susceptible and nothing slows the spread. Blaming the weather alone is the classic mistake: it helps, but the fungus causes the disease.
So for any farm disease, name the cause, then follow the effects from the sick host out to markets and ecosystems. Next, how a plant fights back on its own: a banksia against a root pathogen.
